1.note: Yahweh is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief and warning about the judgment he is about to bring. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas for the shepherds]

1.q: רֹעִ֗ים מְאַבְּדִ֧ים וּ⁠מְפִצִ֛ים אֶת צֹ֥אן מַרְעִיתִ֖⁠י
1.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the leaders of his people as if they were **shepherds** and of his people as if they were **the sheep of my pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders who are destroying and scattering the people for whom I care]

The terms **destroying** and **scattering** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [who are utterly ruining]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 2, 4, 5, 7, 11, 12, 23, 24, and 28–33.

2.q: כֹּֽה אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל עַֽל הָ⁠רֹעִים֮ הָ⁠רֹעִ֣ים אֶת עַמִּ⁠י֒
2.note: Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Here Yahweh is speaking of the leaders of his people as if they were **shepherds** caring for a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the leaders who are caring for my people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a **flock** of sheep that had been driven away from where they belonged. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You, yourselves have driven my people away from their homeland and dispersed them]

The pronoun **You** refers to the leaders of Yahweh’s people, whom he has just called **the shepherds**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You leaders, you are the ones who have scattered my flock]

The pronoun **them** refers to the flock, that is, to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and have driven my flock away, and you have not attended to my people]

2.q: וְ⁠לֹ֥א פְקַדְתֶּ֖ם אֹתָ֑⁠ם הִנְ⁠נִ֨י פֹקֵ֧ד עֲלֵי⁠כֶ֛ם
2.note: Yahweh is using a wordplay here. The same Hebrew word lies behind **attended to** and **attending to**: the shepherds did not attend to the flock, so Yahweh will attend to the shepherds. If your language has a way of repeating a word so that it carries a different sense the second time, you could use it here. If not, you could state the two senses plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have not cared for them. Behold, I am dealing with you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you have done evil deeds]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **deeds** that are characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for your evil deeds]

The terms **scattered** and **driven them away** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [You yourselves have completely driven my flock away]

3.note: Yahweh repeats the pronoun **I** in order to draw a strong contrast between himself and the shepherds who scattered his flock. Use a natural way in your language to express this emphasis. Alternate translation: [And I myself will gather]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a **flock** of sheep that belonged to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the remnant of my people, who are like a flock of sheep to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remnant**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those of my flock who remain]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **remnant** that is what is left of **my flock**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those of my flock who are left]
The pronoun **them** refers to the remnant of Yahweh’s flock, that is, to his people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where I have driven my people]

Here, **the lands** represents the people living in those lands. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from all the countries where the people of my flock have gone]

The pronouns **them** and **they** refer to the remnant of Yahweh’s flock, that is, to the people he will bring back. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will bring that remnant back to their pasture, and those people will be fruitful]

Here Yahweh is speaking of restoring his people to their land as if he were bringing sheep back to **their pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will bring them back to their homeland]

The terms **fruitful** and **multiply** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and they will greatly increase in number]

4.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the leaders he will appoint as if they were **shepherds** who would care for a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will appoint leaders over them, and they will care for them]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here.

The pronoun **they** refers to the new **shepherds** whom Yahweh will raise up, and the pronoun **them** refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and those shepherds will shepherd my people]

The terms **fear** and **be dismayed** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [And they will no longer be terrified]

The pronoun **they** refers to Yahweh’s people, not to the **shepherds** he has just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And my people will no longer fear, and they will not be dismayed]

The expression **will be missing** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. This also occurs in verse 2. Alternate translation: [and none of them will stray away] or [and not will be lost]

5.note: Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Yahweh is using the phrase **days are coming** to introduce what he is about to promise. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Indeed, the time is certainly coming]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a future descendant of David as if he were **a righteous branch** growing out of a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a righteous heir]
See how you translated this phrase in 22:3. This also occurs in verse 5.

6.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Judah will be completely safe, and Israel will dwell securely]

The expression **will be saved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will save Judah]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **safety**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [safely]

Here, **his name** represents the character and the identity of the one who bears it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And people will describe who he is by calling him]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **righteousness** that he gives to his people and that therefore belongs to them. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the one who gives us righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [declares us righteous]

7.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [“As a result,]

Jeremiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

7.q: חַי־יְהוָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֧ר הֶעֱלָ֛ה אֶת־בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל מֵ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם
7.note: Following the custom of his culture, Jeremiah is recording an oath sworn by the people and guaranteeing it by something that they hold sacred. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh, who brought the sons of Israel up from the land of Egypt]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:30.

8.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [but rather they will say]

Jeremiah uses the word **but rather** here to indicate a contrast between what people will no longer say and what they will say instead. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but instead they will say]

8.q: חַי־יְהוָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר הֶעֱלָה֩ וַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵבִ֜יא אֶת־זֶ֨רַע בֵּ֤ית יִשְׂרָאֵל֙
8.note: Following the custom of his culture, Jeremiah is recording an oath in which the people swear by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [As surely as Yahweh lives, who brought up and who led the offspring of the house of Israel … so surely will we tell the truth]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe the **offspring** who belong to **the house of Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the descendants who belong to the house of Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:26.

Jeremiah assumes that readers will know that “the land of the north” refers to Babylon, the land to which the Israelites had been exiled. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [from Babylon, the land to the north]

The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, even though these words are part of what the people will say. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where Yahweh had driven them]

The pronoun **they** refers to the offspring of the house of Israel, whom Yahweh has just mentioned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelites will dwell in their own land]

9.note: Jeremiah is using the phrase translated as **Concerning the prophets** to introduce a new section of his message. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new topic.

Here Jeremiah is speaking of his own deep distress as if his **heart** were an object that could be **broken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am deeply distressed]

The expression **is broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Sorrow has broken my heart]

9.q: הָיִ֨יתִי֙ כְּ⁠אִ֣ישׁ שִׁכּ֔וֹר וּ⁠כְ⁠גֶ֖בֶר עֲבָ֣ר⁠וֹ יָ֑יִן
9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a drunken man** is unsteady and unable to control himself, so is Jeremiah as he takes in what Yahweh has shown him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have become unsteady and unable to control myself, like a drunken man, like a man whom wine has overcome]

Jeremiah is using **because of the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of Yahweh]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **his holy words** as words that are characterized by holiness. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and because of the face of the words he has spoken that are holy]

Jeremiah is again using **because of the face of** as a common expression of the culture, but this time it means “the presence of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and because of the presence of his holy words]

10.note: Jeremiah is using **because of the face of a curse** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of” a curse. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on account of a curse] or [because of a curse]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **curse**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh cursing it]

Jeremiah is speaking of **the land** as if it were a person who could mourn. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land lies desolate]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **the pastures** that are located in **the wilderness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the open grasslands out in the wilderness]

10.q: וַ⁠תְּהִ֤י מְרֽוּצָתָ⁠ם֙ רָעָ֔ה וּ⁠גְבוּרָתָ֖⁠ם לֹא כֵֽן
10.note: The pronoun **Their** refers to the adulterers whom Jeremiah has just mentioned, that is, the prophets and priests who are unfaithful to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The course of the adulterers is evil, and their might is not right]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of the way these people conduct their lives as if it were a **course** that they ran. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their way of living is evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **might**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the way they use their power]

11.q: כִּֽי־גַם־נָבִ֥יא גַם־כֹּהֵ֖ן חָנֵ֑פוּ גַּם־בְּ⁠בֵיתִ֛⁠י מָצָ֥אתִי רָעָתָ֖⁠ם נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה
11.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a first-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a first-level quotation.

The expression **are polluted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [both prophet and priest have defiled themselves]

Here, **prophet** and **priest** represent prophets and priests in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [For the prophets and priests are all polluted]

Here, **my house** represents the temple in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [even in my temple I have found their evil]

12.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result]

The point of this comparison is that just as **slippery places in the darkness** cause a person to lose his footing and fall, so is the course of life of these prophets and priests, which will bring them to ruin. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [their way of life shall lead them to ruin, just as people lose their footing on slippery surfaces in the dark]

Here Yahweh is speaking of how these people live as if it were a **way** along which they walked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their manner of living]

The expression **shall be pushed in** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will push them in, and they shall fall in it]

Yahweh is using **the year of their visitation** as a common expression of the culture to mean the time when he would punish them. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time of their reckoning] or [the time when I will punish them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **visitation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [punishing them]

13.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the prophets** who were living and working in **Samaria**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And among the prophets who lived in Samaria]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **impropriety**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [something improper]

14.q: וְ⁠חִזְּקוּ֙ יְדֵ֣י מְרֵעִ֔ים לְ⁠בִ֨לְתִּי־שָׁ֔בוּ אִ֖ישׁ מֵ⁠רָֽעָת֑⁠וֹ
14.note: The words translated as **so that** indicate that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [And they have strengthened the hands of evildoers. As a result, no man turns back from his evil]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the prophets** who were living and working in **Jerusalem**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. This also occurs in verse 15. Alternate translation: [And among the prophets who live in Jerusalem]

The expressions **committing adultery** and **walking in falsehood** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [utterly unfaithful living]

Here Yahweh is speaking of living in a habitual way as if it were **walking** along a path. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and habitually living deceitfully]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 25, 26, and 32. Alternate translation: [deceitfully]

Yahweh is using **strengthened the hands of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “encouraged.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they have emboldened evildoers]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [so that no person turns back from his or her evil]

14.q: הָֽיוּ לִ֤⁠י כֻלָּ⁠ם֙ כִּ⁠סְדֹ֔ם וְ⁠יֹשְׁבֶ֖י⁠הָ כַּ⁠עֲמֹרָֽה
14.note: Jeremiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [All of them have become to me like Sodom, and her inhabitants have become to me like Gomorrah]

14.q: הָֽיוּ לִ֤⁠י כֻלָּ⁠ם֙ כִּ⁠סְדֹ֔ם וְ⁠יֹשְׁבֶ֖י⁠הָ כַּ⁠עֲמֹרָֽה
14.note: The point of this comparison is that just as the people of **Sodom** and **Gomorrah** were thoroughly corrupt and deserving of judgment, so are these prophets and the people of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [All of the prophets have become to me as thoroughly corrupt as Sodom was, and her inhabitants have become as deserving of judgment as was Gomorrah]
The pronoun **her** refers to Jerusalem, not to Sodom. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the inhabitants of Jerusalem]

15.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Since the prophets of Jerusalem have done these things]

15.q: כֹּֽה אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ עַל הַ⁠נְּבִאִ֔ים
15.note: Jeremiah is using **thus says Yahweh of Armies** to indicate that what follows is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. See how you translated the similar expression in 6:6. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language. See the UST.

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to make them eat wormwood]

Yahweh is speaking as if the water they would drink were **poison**, meaning that he will cause suffering to come to the prophets. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and causing them to suffer as if it were poisoned water that they drank]
See how you translated **the prophets of Jerusalem** in 23:14.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pollution**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what defiles]

16.note: See how you translated **Thus says Yahweh of Armies** in 23:15.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the words** that come from **the prophets** themselves. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the words that the prophets speak]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the inner thoughts of these prophets as if their **heart** were the place their visions came from. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a vision that they themselves have made up]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **a vision** that originates in the **heart** of these prophets rather than in a message from him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a vision that they themselves have imagined]

Yahweh is using **the mouth** to represent himself as the one who speaks. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [not from Yahweh himself]

17.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the false prophets whom Yahweh described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. This also occurs in verse 38. Alternate translation: [Those prophets keep saying]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the same Hebrew verb in **Saying, they say** in order to emphasize that these prophets say this again and again. If your language can repeat words for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here. If not, you could express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Again and again they say]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You will be safe]

Here the masculine term **his** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [And to everyone, whether man or woman, walking in the stubbornness of his or her heart]

Jeremiah is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And to everyone who lives according to the stubbornness of his heart]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **stubbornness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to everyone who stubbornly walks according to what his own heart desires]

The pronoun **you** refers to the people who stubbornly do whatever they want, to whom these prophets are speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Disaster will not come upon you who are stubborn]

18.q: כִּ֣י מִ֤י עָמַד֙ בְּ⁠ס֣וֹד יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠יֵ֖רֶא וְ⁠יִשְׁמַ֣ע אֶת־דְּבָר֑⁠וֹ מִֽי־הִקְשִׁ֥יב דבר⁠י וַ⁠יִּשְׁמָֽע
18.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that none of these prophets has stood in Yahweh’s counsel or received his word. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one has stood in the counsel of Yahweh and seen and heard his word! No one has paid attention to his word and listened!]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **the counsel** that **Yahweh** gives to those who stand before him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in the place where Yahweh gives advice]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **his word** as the message that comes from Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the message that comes from him]

Jeremiah is using the question form to emphasize that no one among these prophets has truly paid attention to what Yahweh says. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For no one has stood in the counsel of Yahweh and seen and heard his word! No one has paid attention to his word and listened!]

19.note: Jeremiah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of Yahweh’s judgment as if it were **a storm** that swept everything before it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is punishing with destructive force, like a storm]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **a storm** that **Yahweh** sends. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a storm that Yahweh is sending]

Jeremiah is using **Wrath has gone out** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh’s wrath is about to be unleashed against the wicked. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Wrath is being unleashed] or [Wrath is about to strike]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **Wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The wrathful Yahweh]

Jeremiah is using **the head** to represent the whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [upon the wicked themselves it will whirl]

Jeremiah is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the wicked people]

20.note: Jeremiah is speaking of the **nose** of Yahweh as if it were a living thing that could turn back. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not cease from wrathful actions]

Jeremiah is using **The nose of Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the anger of Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The anger of Yahweh will not cease]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **turn back**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s anger will continue]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of what Yahweh purposes to do as if his **heart** were the place where those purposes were formed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he purposes to do]

Jeremiah is using the possessive form to describe **the intentions** that come from Yahweh’s **heart**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he intends in his heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **intentions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he intends in his heart]

Jeremiah is using the phrase **In the latter days** to indicate that what follows will happen at a time still to come. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Later on]

Yahweh is using a verb and a noun from the same Hebrew root in **understand it with understanding** in order to emphasize how clearly the people will see this. If your language can repeat related words for emphasis, it would be appropriate to do that here. If not, you could express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you will understand it completely]
The pronoun **it** refers to the purpose of Yahweh that Jeremiah has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you will understand Yahweh’s purpose]

21.note: Yahweh repeats the pronoun **they** twice in order to draw a strong contrast between the prophets and himself, who did not send them. Use a natural way in your language to express this emphasis. Alternate translation: [yet those prophets ran anyway … yet those prophets prophesied anyway]

22.note: Yahweh is making a conditional statement that sounds hypothetical, but he knows that the condition is not true. He is stating it as a condition to show that what follows, that these prophets turned his people back from their evil, is also not true. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that the speaker believes is not true. Alternate translation: [But if they actually had stood in my counsel, which they did not]

Jeremiah is using **stood in my counsel** as a common expression of the culture to mean “sought my counsel” or “followed my counsel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they had met with me] or [they had listened to me]

Here Yahweh is speaking of how these people live as if it were a **evil way** along which they walked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from their evil behavior]

23.q: הַ⁠אֱלֹהֵ֧י מִ⁠קָּרֹ֛ב אָ֖נִי נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה וְ⁠לֹ֥א אֱלֹהֵ֖י מֵ⁠רָחֹֽק
23.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he is present everywhere and not only nearby. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am not only a God who is near,” declares Yahweh, “I am also a God who is far away!]

24.q: אִם יִסָּתֵ֨ר אִ֧ישׁ בַּ⁠מִּסְתָּרִ֛ים וַ⁠אֲנִ֥י לֹֽא אֶרְאֶ֖⁠נּוּ
24.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to hide from him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [A man certainly cannot hide himself in secret places so that I will not see him!]

Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a man or a woman hide himself or herself]

Yahweh is using **in secret places** as a common expression of the culture to mean a place where no one else could see or find a person. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [somewhere he thinks I cannot see him] or [in a place where no one else could find him]

24.q: הֲ⁠ל֨וֹא אֶת הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֧יִם וְ⁠אֶת הָ⁠אָ֛רֶץ אֲנִ֥י מָלֵ֖א
24.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he is present everywhere. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I certainly fill the heavens and the earth!]

Yahweh is referring to all of creation by naming its two major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that exists]

25.note: Here, **my name** represents Yahweh’s own authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones prophesying falsehood by my authority]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe prophesying that is done by claiming **my name** as its authority. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones prophesying falsehood while claiming that I authorized them]

The prophets are repeating the words **I have dreamed** in order to intensify their expression of the idea that those words convey. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I have certainly dreamed]

26.q: עַד־מָתַ֗י הֲ⁠יֵ֛שׁ בְּ⁠לֵ֥ב הַ⁠נְּבִאִ֖ים נִבְּאֵ֣י הַ⁠שָּׁ֑קֶר וּ⁠נְבִיאֵ֖י תַּרְמִ֥ת לִבָּֽ⁠ם
26.note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke these prophets for continuing to proclaim what they have invented. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. See the UST.

Here Yahweh is speaking of the intentions of these prophets as if their **heart** were a container that held them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what the prophets intend]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the prophets** who are characterized by **the deceit of their heart**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the prophets whose hearts are deceitful]

Jeremiah is speaking of the **heart** as if it were the source of the deceit in the prophets, representing the thoughts and intentions that produce their false prophecies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the prophets who prophesy the lies that they have deceitfully thought up]

27.note: Here, **my name** represents Yahweh himself and the worship that belongs to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to make my people forget me and stop worshiping me]

Jeremiah is using **a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each man.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each man] or [each one]

As in the first part of this verse, **my name** here represents Yahweh himself and the loyalty that his people owe him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their fathers abandoned me on account of Baal]

Here the masculine term **fathers** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [their forefathers and foremothers]

28.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize how completely unlike his own word the dreams of these prophets are. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Chaff has nothing in common with grain!]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [What does the straw have in common with the grain]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the dreams of these prophets as if they were **straw** and of his own word as if it were **the grain**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do these prophets’ worthless dreams have in common with my valuable word]

29.q: הֲ⁠ל֨וֹא כֹ֧ה דְבָרִ֛⁠י כָּ⁠אֵ֖שׁ & וּ⁠כְ⁠פַטִּ֖ישׁ יְפֹ֥צֵֽץ סָֽלַע
29.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize the power of his word. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My word is surely like fire!” declares Yahweh. “And it is surely like a hammer that shatters a rock!]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fire** consumes what it burns and **a hammer** breaks apart what it strikes, so is the word of Yahweh in its power to accomplish what he sends it to do. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as powerful as fire to consume whatever it touches” —says Yahweh— “and as powerful as a hammer that shatters a rock]

30.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because of that]

Yahweh is using **behold me against the prophets** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he strongly opposes and will punish the prophets. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I strongly oppose the prophets] or [I am against the prophets]

Here Yahweh is speaking of these prophets repeating one another’s messages as if they were **stealing** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones taking my words for themselves]

31.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me against the prophets** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am opposed to the prophets.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look, I am against the prophets] or [I am opposed to the prophets]

Yahweh is using **their tongue** to represent their speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones using their own words]

Yahweh is using a verb and a noun from the same Hebrew root in **declaring a declaration** in order to mock the way these prophets speak. If your language can repeat related words in this way, it would be appropriate to do that here. If not, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and announcing their own announcements]

32.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **dreams** that are characterized by **falsehood**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [false dreams]

The terms **falsehoods** and **recklessness** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [by their utterly reckless lies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recklessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and because they act recklessly]

Yahweh repeats the pronoun **I** in order to draw a contrast between himself and these prophets, who claim to speak for him. Use a natural way in your language to express this emphasis. Alternate translation: [yet I myself did not send them]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **benefit** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [So they will certainly not benefit this people at all]

33.q: וְ⁠כִי יִשְׁאָלְ⁠ךָ֩ הָ⁠עָ֨ם הַ⁠זֶּ֜ה אֽוֹ הַ⁠נָּבִ֤יא אֽוֹ כֹהֵן֙
33.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible situation, that this people or a prophet or a priest might ask Jeremiah about **the burden of Yahweh**. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [And if this people, or a prophet, or a priest should ask you]

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “What is the burden of Yahweh? Then you shall say to them, ‘What burden?’” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “You are the burden, and I will abandon you.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Yahweh is using a wordplay here. The Hebrew word translated as **burden** means both “a message that a prophet carries” and “a heavy load.” The people ask for a message, and Yahweh answers by telling them that they themselves are the load he will put down. If your language has a single word with both senses, you could use it here. If not, you could translate each occurrence with the sense that fits and explain the wordplay in a footnote.

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the burden** as a message that comes from him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 34, 36, and 38. Alternate translation: [is the burden that Yahweh has declared]

The pronoun **you** refers to Jeremiah, while the pronoun **them** refers to whichever person from the people, or the prophet, or the priest, asks the question. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [then you, Jeremiah, shall say to that person]

34.note: Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [that person and their household]

35.q: אִ֥ישׁ עַל רֵעֵ֖⁠הוּ וְ⁠אִ֣ישׁ אֶל אָחִ֑י⁠ו
35.note: Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person to his neighbor and each person to his relative]

35.q: מֶה עָנָ֣ה יְהוָ֔ה וּ⁠מַה דִּבֶּ֖ר יְהוָֽה
35.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [What has Yahweh answered, that is, what has Yahweh spoken]

36.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **word** that comes from a person himself rather than from Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the word that each man himself has spoken]

Here the masculine term **each man’s** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [each person’s own word]

Here Yahweh is speaking of misrepresenting his message as if the people had **perverted** it by twisting it out of shape. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for you have misrepresented the words of the living God]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the words** that come from **the living God**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the words that the living God has spoken]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:3.

37.note: Yahweh is using **Thus you say to the prophet** to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

38.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible situation, that someone might say **The burden of Yahweh**. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [But whenever you say, “The burden of Yahweh,”]

39.q: הִנְ⁠נִ֔י וְ⁠נָשִׁ֥יתִי אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם נָשֹׁ֑א וְ⁠נָטַשְׁתִּ֣י אֶתְ⁠כֶ֗ם
39.note: The terms **forget** and **abandon** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [behold, I will surely banish you]

Yahweh is using **behold me, I will surely forget you** as a common expression of the culture to emphasize that what he is about to say will certainly happen. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [listen, I will definitely forget you] or [I will forget you, without a doubt]

The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh, and the pronoun **you** refers to the people of Jerusalem to whom he is speaking. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [behold, I, Yahweh, will surely forget you people]
Here, **my face** represents Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from my presence]

40.note: The terms **everlasting reproach** and **everlasting shame** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [everlasting disgrace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [perpetual reproaching and perpetual shaming]

Yahweh says **that will not be forgotten** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [that people will remember always]

The expression **will not be forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that no one will ever forget]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **forgotten**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [that people will always remember]
